name: attention_scarcity_vs_freedom_of_expression
description: Does freedom of expression logically require a limit on attention, because attention received by a few restricts the effective freedom of expression of everyone else? Dataset of the argument structure (premises, counter-positions) with measured attention-concentration and amplification figures from verified studies. Measured values are untagged (default); conjectures from the dialogue carry the tag 'assumed' with a confidence number 0 to 1. Original request (German): 'muesste Meinungsfreiheit nicht auch gleichzeitig bedeuten, dass es eine Begrenzung der Aufmerksamkeit braucht, denn wenn einzelne Menschen viel Aufmerksamkeit erhalten, schraenkt dies die Meinungsfreiheit der anderen ein' followed by 'ja, gerne ein json vor allem mit studien und zahlen'.

words.name: freedom of expression
words.description: the right to express opinions without state interference; the classical negative liberty protected by Art. 16 of the Swiss Federal Constitution and Art. 10 ECHR.

words.name: negative freedom
words.description: freedom from interference: nobody may stop you from speaking.

words.name: effective freedom
words.description: positive or effective freedom: the real capacity to be heard, not only to speak.

words.name: right to an audience
words.description: a hypothetical entitlement to be listened to; not part of the classical freedom of expression.

words.name: freedom of information
words.description: the listener-side freedom to receive information from any source of one's choice (Art. 16 para. 3 Swiss Federal Constitution).

words.name: attention
words.description: the finite cognitive resource of an audience; what receivers allocate to messages.

words.name: attention scarcity
words.description: the condition that a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention (Simon 1971).

words.name: attention concentration
words.description: the degree to which a small share of speakers receives a large share of total attention.

words.name: attention cap
words.description: the proposal from the dialogue: an upper limit on the attention a single speaker may receive.

words.name: allocating authority
words.description: an institution that would have to measure and distribute attention if a cap were enforced.

words.name: reach
words.description: the number of people a message is actually shown to; distinct from the right to speak (DiResta: free speech is not free reach).

words.name: algorithmic amplification
words.description: increase of a message's reach caused by ranked, personalized feeds relative to a chronological feed.

words.name: amplification ratio
words.description: reach on ranked timelines divided by reach on chronological timelines minus one, in percent (Huszar 2022); 0% means equal reach, 100% means double reach.

words.name: chronological feed
words.description: a feed showing posts from followed accounts in reverse time order without algorithmic personalization.

words.name: ranked feed
words.description: a feed ordered by an engagement-optimizing personalization algorithm.

words.name: social influence
words.description: the effect of seeing other people's choices on one's own choices; increases inequality and unpredictability of success (Salganik 2006).

words.name: network effect
words.description: the winner-take-all dynamic in which value and audience grow with existing audience size.

words.name: middleware
words.description: a competitive layer of third-party curation services that lets users choose their own feed ranking (Fukuyama 2021).

words.name: antitrust
words.description: competition law that limits abuse of market power without capping success itself.

words.name: media concentration law
words.description: rules limiting ownership concentration in the media sector to preserve plurality.

words.name: Fairness Doctrine
words.description: US broadcast rule (1949 to 1987) requiring balanced coverage on scarce spectrum; a historical precedent for regulating attention distribution rather than speech.

words.name: regulate reach mechanism
words.description: the alternative proposed in the dialogue: regulate the mechanisms that distribute attention (ranking, paid reach, transparency, interoperability) instead of capping attention.

words.name: libertarian position
words.description: counter-position: reach is simply success with the audience and any regulation is paternalism.

words.name: deliberative democracy position
words.description: counter-position (Habermas tradition): a functioning public sphere must not be left to the market; active structuring is legitimate.

words.name: attention is approximately zero-sum
words.description: claim: because attention is finite, attention gained by one speaker is lost to others.

words.name: attention cap restricts listeners more than speakers
words.description: claim: an attention cap would mainly restrict the many who choose to listen, not the one who is listened to.

words.name: attention cap requires allocating authority
words.description: claim: an enforceable cap needs an institution that measures and distributes attention.

words.name: regulating reach mechanisms preserves both freedoms
words.description: claim: regulating ranking, paid reach, transparency and interoperability addresses concentration while preserving speaker and listener freedom.

words.name: algorithms are the primary cause of concentration
words.description: claim: algorithmic ranking, not audience preference, is the main driver of attention concentration; contested because Wu 2011 predates ranked feeds and Salganik 2006 shows social influence alone creates inequality.

words.name: middleware reduces concentration
words.description: claim: a competitive curation layer would measurably reduce attention concentration.

triples.description: Huszar 2022: in 6 of 7 countries the mainstream right had statistically significantly higher amplification than the mainstream left; no evidence that far-left or far-right groups were amplified more than moderates.

triples.name: false news influences reach
triples.description: Vosoughi 2018: falsehood diffused farther, faster, deeper and more broadly than truth in all categories; bots spread both at the same rate, so humans drive the difference.

triples.name: chronological feed experiment influences attention
triples.description: Guess 2023: moving users to a chronological feed substantially decreased time on platform, increased exposure to political and untrustworthy content, decreased uncivil content on Facebook, and did not significantly change issue polarization, affective polarization or political knowledge within 3 months.

triples.name: attention scarcity of attention
triples.description: Simon 1971: what information consumes is the attention of its recipients; a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention.

triples.name: middleware influences reach
triples.description: Fukuyama 2021: outsourcing curation to competitive middleware companies as the more promising remedy compared to antitrust breakup, content regulation, data portability and privacy law alone.

triples.name: libertarian position influences attention cap
triples.description: counter-position rejecting any cap or reach regulation.

triples.name: deliberative democracy position influences regulate reach mechanism
triples.description: counter-position supporting active structuring of the public sphere.
